e-6106.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
e-6106.problem: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,1] \times [1,2].$
e-6106.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  xy\  e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\  e^{x}  \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot  \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &=  \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &= e^2
}
$$

e-6107.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
e-6107.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{-1}^{3}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-(-1)){\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{4}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{224}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A=3\,\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot (2\cdot 4)=24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}A=\frac{56}{3}-\frac{224}{3}+24=-32.\end{aligned}
$$

e-7023.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
\iint\limits_{C}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = 8,
\qquad
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = -5,
$$

find the value of 

$$
\iint\limits_{C \cup D}  3f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$
e-7023.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(8+(-5)) \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

e-6108.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain
e-6108.problem:
Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A$, where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054242/assets/d96ec9ab40f8f1cadd6d2492dddcc0090f766b72e9c7fdb659e3b2f7f39fce0d.png)
and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
e-6108.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2,$ where $R_1= (0,2) \times (-1,0)$ and $R_2= (0,2) \times (0,1).$ So, we can write

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 2 \ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{R_2}    \dfrac{1}{xy+x+y+1} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2\iint\limits_{R_1} \textrm d A
+ \iint\limits_{R_2}  \dfrac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2(2-0)(0-(-1)) + \Bigg( \int_0^2 \dfrac{1}{x+1} \ \textrm d x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{y+1}\ \textrm d y \Bigg) \[5pt]
&= 4 + \Big[\ln(x+1)\Big]_0^2  \cdot \Big[\ln(y+1)\Big]_0^1\[5pt] 
&= 4+ \ln 3\ln 2.
}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[0,\pi ]\times [0,2].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(\frac{1}{4+{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi }\cdot [\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{2})]_{0}^{2} \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{8}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{{e}^{y}}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,\sqrt{3}]\times [0,1].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{{e}^{y}}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}})({e}^{y})\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot [{e}^{y}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡1)\cdot ({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot (e-1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}(e-1)\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
content.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{{e}^{y}}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,\sqrt{3}]\times [0,1].$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{{e}^{y}}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}})({e}^{y})\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot [{e}^{y}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡1)\cdot ({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot (e-1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}(e-1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(6{x}^{2}-10{y}^{4})\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}6{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}10{y}^{4}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{-2}^{0}6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot 2{x}^{3}{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =2(2\cdot {0}^{3}-2\cdot (-2)^{3}) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}10{y}^{4}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-2)){\int }_{-1}^{1}10{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot 2{y}^{5}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2(2\cdot {1}^{5}-2\cdot (-1)^{5}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(6{x}^{2}+10{y}^{4})\,\text{d}A=32-8=24.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{2+6y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,2]\times [2,4].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{2+6y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}6y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{2}{x}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{2}{2}-(-\frac{2}{1})) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{2}^{4}6y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3{y}^{2}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =3({4}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{2+6y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=2+36=38.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}(4{y}^{3}-2x)\text{d}A$,  where $R=[2,5]\times [0,3].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(4{y}^{3}-2x)\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}4{y}^{3}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}2x\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}4{y}^{3}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(5-2){\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[{y}^{4}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =3({3}^{4}-{0}^{4}) \\  & =243.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{2}^{5}2x\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[{x}^{2}]_{2}^{5} \\  & =3({5}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =63.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(4{y}^{3}-2x)\,\text{d}A=243-63=180.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [0,2].$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A=2\,\text{Area}(R)=2\cdot (3\cdot 2)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2({3}^{2}-(0)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2y\,\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot [{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3({2}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=12+18-24=6.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2},\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=\frac{3}{2},
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{f(x,y)}{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{f(x,y)}{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}0, & (x,y)\in S, \\ \frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}, & (x,y)\in T, \\ \frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}

$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{T}\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬S0dA+∬Tx1+y2dA+∬Uy1+x2dA=∬Tx1+y2dA+∬Uy1+x2dA.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms additivity over S, T, and U. The integral over S is zero, leaving the integral of x/(1+y²) over T plus the integral of y/(1+x²) over U, exactly option b.

{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=

content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{T}\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=12,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-8,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(12-8) \\  & =12\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Using Additivity of Double Integrals
content.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=12,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-8,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(12-8) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ycos⁡x,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,ex+y,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA
b
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬TdA+∬Uex+ydA
c
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Uex+ydA
d
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA+∬UdA
e
 ∬Sex+ydA+∬Uycos⁡xdA
Submit

decision.explanation: By additivity, sum the integrals over S, T, and U using each region's formula. Since f=0 on T, its contribution vanishes, leaving the integrals of y cos(x) over S and e^(x+y) over U.

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, & (x,y)\in S, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in T, \\ {e}^{x+y}, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

a
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA
b
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬TdA+∬Uex+ydA
c
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Uex+ydA
d
 ∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Tex+ydA+∬UdA
e
 ∬Sex+ydA+∬Uycos⁡xdA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬T0dA+∬Uex+ydA=∬Sycos⁡xdA+∬Uex+ydA.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms additivity over S, T, and U. Since f=0 on T, only the integral of y cos(x) over S and the integral of e^(x+y) over U remain, giving option c.

$$

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={x,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,x2y,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬SxdA+∬Ux2ydA
b
∬SxdA+∬Tx2ydA
c
∬TxdA+∬Ux2ydA
d
∬SxdA+∬TydA+∬Ux2ydA
e
∬SxdA+∬T(x+x2y)dA+∬Ux2ydA
Submit

decision.explanation: By additivity, integrate each piece over its region. The contribution from T is zero, leaving the integral of x over S plus the integral of x²y over U.

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}x, & (x,y)\in S, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in T, \\ {x}^{2}y, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={x,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,x2y,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬SxdA+∬Ux2ydA
b
∬SxdA+∬Tx2ydA
c
∬TxdA+∬Ux2ydA
d
∬SxdA+∬TydA+∬Ux2ydA
e
∬SxdA+∬T(x+x2y)dA+∬Ux2ydA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬SxdA+∬T0dA+∬Ux2ydA=∬SxdA+∬Ux2ydA.

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}x, & (x,y)\in S, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in T, \\ {x}^{2}y, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Split the domain into its two rectangles. The first contributes 8∫₋₁¹ 3y² dy = 16. The second contributes (1/4)(∫₁⁹ x^(−1/2) dx)(∫₁⁴ y^(−1/2) dy) = (1/4)·4·2 = 2. The total is 18.

EXPLANATION

First, notice that we have R=R1∪R2, where R1=(1,9)×(−1,1) and R2=(1,9)×(1,4). So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA==∬R1f(x,y)dA+∬R2f(x,y)dA=∬R13y2dA+∬R214xydA=∬R13y2dA+∬R2(12x)(12y)dA=(9−1)∫−113y2dy+(∫1912xdx)(∫1412ydy)=8[y3]−11+[x]19⋅[y]14=8(13−(−1)3)+(3−1)⋅(2−1)=18.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms that the two rectangles contribute 8(1−(−1)) = 16 and (√9−√1)(√4−√1) = 2. Their sum is 18, so option c is correct.

$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(1,2)\times ((1,2)\cup (2,4)) \\  & =((1,2)\times (1,2))\cup ((1,2)\times (2,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,1<y<2, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,2<y<4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,4)}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(1,2)\times ((1,2)\cup (2,4)) \\  & =((1,2)\times (1,2))\cup ((1,2)\times (2,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ycos⁡x,if0<x<π,0<y<π4,xsec2⁡y,if0<x<π,π4<y<π2. Then, ∬(0,π)×(0,π/2)f(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬(0,π)×(0,π/4)xsec2⁡ydA+∬(0,π)×(π/4,π/2)ycos⁡xdA
b
 ∬(0,π)×(0,π/2)(ycos⁡x+xsec2⁡y)dA
c
 ∫(0,π)xcos⁡xdx+∫(0,π/2)ysec2⁡ydy
d
 ∬(0,π)×(0,π/4)ycos⁡xdA+∬(0,π)×(π/4,π/2)xsec2⁡ydA
e
 ∬(0,π/2)×(0,π/2)ycos⁡xdA+∬(π/2,π)×(0,π/2)xsec2⁡ydA
Submit

decision.explanation: Split at y=π/4 and use each formula on its defining rectangle, giving option d. The second integral diverges to +∞ because ∫ sec²(y) dy = tan(y) grows without bound as y approaches π/2; the equality holds as an improper integral.

after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(0,\pi )\times ((0,\frac{\pi }{4})\cup (\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =((0,\pi )\times (0,\frac{\pi }{4}))\cup ((0,\pi )\times (\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (0,\pi /4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (\pi /4,\pi /2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (0,\pi /4)}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (\pi /4,\pi /2)}\sqrt{x}{sec}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(0,\pi )\times ((0,\frac{\pi }{4})\cup (\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =((0,\pi )\times (0,\frac{\pi }{4}))\cup ((0,\pi )\times (\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (0,\pi /4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (\pi /4,\pi /2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (0,\pi /4)}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(0,\pi )\times (\pi /4,\pi /2)}\sqrt{x}{sec}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
